The transmission distribution analysis demonstrated that higher-voltage facilities contributed more to interzonal power flows and, therefore, higher regional utilization than lower-voltage facilities. In a follow-up study to the transmission distribution analysis, SPP conducted an injection withdrawal transmission utilization analysis, which estimates the utilization rate for transmission facilities for local utilization or “other” utilization, which indicates general regional usage. To perform the analysis, SPP used a unit-commitment economic dispatch model representing the existing topology of the SPP system. The average utilization of high-voltage transmission facilities across all hours in the analysis was 78%, indicating high-voltage facilities predominantly support regional transmission services and lower-voltage facilities serve local transmission services (SPP 2010a). SPP filed the results of these studies with their application to FERC for tariff revisions to adopt the Highway/Byway cost allocation methodology (Order Accepting Tariff Revisions 2010). The Highway/Byway method and the preceding processes, studies, and stakeholder groups represent a unique approach to ex ante cost allocation. SPP performed a rigorous analytical study of the system topology and power flows to justify an ex ante regional cost allocation method that allocates costs to network users or beneficiaries without the need for detailed study of each project. This cost allocation method would apply to all future transmission upgrades, regardless of the underlying project driver. C.4 PJM Artificial Island Project The PJM Artificial Island Project was recommended to the board in a white paper to resolve stability issues identified by PJM at the Salem and Hope Creek nuclear plants in New Jersey and to relieve congestion on the Delmarva Peninsula. LS Power was awarded the competitive bid to build the transmission line, and Public Service Electric & Gas and Pepco Holdings were tasked with upgrading the substations on either end (RTO Insider 2020). The project consisted of 12 transmission enhancements, 5 would operate above a threshold of 500-kV or 345-kV double circuit, and the remaining 7 were planned below this threshold, including a 3-mile 230-kV underwater cable beneath the Delaware River. PJM opened its first Order 1000 Regional Transmission Expansion Planning (RTEP) process window in April 2013. Under its approved Order 1000 tariff for cost allocation for regional facilities, the costs of transmission facilities greater than 500 kV or double-circuit 345 kV would be allocated 50% to the region on a load ratio share basis and 50% using the distribution factor analysis method, or DFAX method (PJM 2010). For lower-voltage facilities, 100% of the costs are allocated using the DFAX method. The DFAX method is intended to measure each transmission zone’s use of the upgrade to serve zonal load through changes in power flows.
